lead: A radar beam also hits the ground, the sea, buildings and hills, and their echoes, called clutter, can be thousands of times stronger than an aircraft. Fixed clutter has no Doppler shift, while a moving target does. Moving target indication (MTI) compares successive pulses and cancels whatever has not changed; pulse Doppler radar goes further and sorts echoes into Doppler bins, so it also measures speed. The price is a set of blind speeds fixed by the wavelength and the PRF. Airport surveillance radars, weather radars and fighter radars all depend on these ideas.
prereq: You need the Doppler shift fd = 2vr/λ from CW and FMCW radar and the PRF from Pulse repetition frequency and range ambiguities.

sections.h3: Clutter and the coherent MTI radar

blocks.text: Clutter can be 40 to 60 dB stronger than an aircraft echo, so no threshold can pass the aircraft and stop the ground. The Doppler shift separates them. Fixed clutter (ground, buildings) has f<sub>d</sub> ≈ 0. Sea and rain clutter move with waves and wind, so they have a small Doppler spread that is often off zero; they are harder to cancel.

A pulse radar sees Doppler as a change of phase from pulse to pulse. A coherent MTI radar keeps a phase reference for this. A stable local oscillator (STALO) and a coherent oscillator (COHO) at the intermediate frequency drive the transmitter chain; on receive, a phase detector compares each echo with the COHO. A fixed target gives the same output on every pulse; a moving target's output changes by 2π f<sub>d</sub>T<sub>r</sub> radians from one pulse to the next.

The comparison is done separately for every range gate: the sample at delay 2R/c from one pulse is compared with the sample at the same delay from the previous pulse, exactly one pulse interval T<sub>r</sub> earlier. A magnetron starts with a random phase on each pulse, so a magnetron radar either locks its COHO to each transmitted pulse or uses noncoherent MTI, which uses the clutter itself as the reference.
A single delay-line canceller subtracts the previous pulse's output from the present one. Fixed echoes cancel; a moving target leaves a residue whose size depends on f<sub>d</sub>:

|H(fd)| = 2 |sin(π fd Tr)|
Here H is the voltage response of the canceller (input amplitude 1); fd is the Doppler shift in Hz; Tr = 1/PRF is the pulse interval in s.

The response is zero whenever f<sub>d</sub> = n·PRF: the target then moves a whole number of half-wavelengths between pulses, its phase returns to the same value, and it cancels like clutter. The radial speeds at which this happens are the blind speeds:

blocks.where: v<sub>b</sub> is the n-th blind speed in m/s, n = 1, 2, 3, …; λ is the wavelength in m; PRF is in Hz.

blocks.text: The response peaks at 2 when f<sub>d</sub> is an odd multiple of PRF/2. A double canceller (two in cascade) has |H| = 4 sin²(π f<sub>d</sub> T<sub>r</sub>): its notch around zero is wider, so it rejects clutter with some spread better, but it also loses more of the slow targets. The quality of an MTI is given by its improvement factor: the signal-to-clutter ratio at the output divided by that at the input, averaged over all target speeds, in dB.

Staggered PRF changes T<sub>r</sub> from pulse to pulse. A target is then blind only if its speed is blind at every interval. With two intervals in the ratio T<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>2</sub> = a/b (whole numbers), the first common blind Doppler is a/T<sub>1</sub>, so the first blind speed rises to (a + b)/2 times the blind speed of a constant PRF with the average interval. The figure shows this for the second worked example. The cost: clutter cancellation is a little poorer, and the processing must allow for the changing interval.

sections.h3: Pulse Doppler radar and the MTD

blocks.text: A pulse Doppler radar sends a burst of N coherent pulses on each beam position and passes each range gate through a bank of N Doppler filters, usually an FFT. Each filter is PRF/N wide in Doppler; clutter falls in the filters near zero and is thrown away, and the filter with the largest output gives the target's speed. The result is a range-Doppler map.

For example, N = 16 pulses at PRF = 10 kHz give filters 10 000/16 = 625 Hz wide; at λ = 3 cm that is 625 × 0.03/2 = 9.4 m/s per filter, with speeds unambiguous over ±75 m/s. The same 10 kHz PRF leaves only 15 km of unambiguous range, which is why pulse Doppler radars use medium or high PRF and resolve range with several PRFs.

The moving target detector (MTD), used in airport surveillance radars, combines the two: a short canceller, then a small Doppler filter bank, with a separate threshold for each filter and a clutter map for the zero-Doppler filter. In short:

items: MTI removes fixed clutter; it does not measure speed.
Pulse Doppler measures speed from which filter is strongest.
Blind speeds come from the Doppler sampling by the PRF; range ambiguity comes from the listening time.

examples.question: An X-band MTI radar has λ = 3 cm and PRF = 1000 Hz. Find the first two blind speeds in m/s and km/h, and the canceller response for a target closing at 10 m/s.
examples.answer: Blind speeds 15 m/s (54 km/h) and 30 m/s (108 km/h); a 10 m/s target passes with gain 1.73, nearly the peak of 2.

examples.question: The radar staggers its PRF between 1000 Hz and 1250 Hz. Find the blind speeds of each PRF alone, the first blind speed of the staggered radar, and the response of each interval for a target at 15 m/s.
steps: Alone: v<sub>b</sub> = λ·PRF/2 = 0.03 × 1000/2 = 15 m/s and 0.03 × 1250/2 = 18.75 m/s (with all their multiples).
Intervals: T<sub>1</sub> = 1 ms, T<sub>2</sub> = 0.8 ms, ratio T<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>2</sub> = 5/4, so a = 5, b = 4.
First common blind Doppler: a/T<sub>1</sub> = 5/1 ms = 5000 Hz, and b/T<sub>2</sub> = 4/0.8 ms = 5000 Hz, the same.
v<sub>b</sub> = 5000 × 0.03/2 = 75 m/s. Check with (a + b)/2: the average interval is 0.9 ms, whose blind speed is 0.03/(2 × 0.9 × 10⁻³) = 16.67 m/s, and 4.5 × 16.67 = 75 m/s.
At 15 m/s, f<sub>d</sub> = 1000 Hz: the 1 ms interval gives 2|sin(π)| = 0, but the 0.8 ms interval gives 2|sin(0.8π)| = 1.18, so the target is still seen.
examples.answer: Alone the blind speeds are 15 and 18.75 m/s; staggered, the first blind speed moves out to 75 m/s (270 km/h), and the 15 m/s target is passed at 1.18 on alternate intervals.

traps: Saying MTI measures speed. A canceller only removes fixed clutter; speed needs a Doppler filter bank.
Mixing up blind speed and blind Doppler frequency. The blind frequencies are n·PRF in Hz; the blind speeds are nλ·PRF/2 in m/s.
Putting λ in centimetres into v<sub>b</sub> = nλ·PRF/2.
Saying clutter always has zero Doppler. Rain and sea clutter move with the wind and waves.
Assuming a double canceller is always better. Its wider notch rejects more clutter but also more slow targets.

quiz.q: A single canceller has T<sub>r</sub> = 0.5 ms. At which Doppler frequencies is its response zero?
quiz.a: At f<sub>d</sub> = n/T<sub>r</sub> = n × 2000 Hz: 0, 2000, 4000 Hz, …

quiz.q: Define the improvement factor of an MTI radar.
quiz.a: The output signal-to-clutter ratio divided by the input signal-to-clutter ratio, averaged over target speeds, usually in dB.

quiz.q: Why does a fixed amplitude threshold fail against ground clutter?
quiz.a: Clutter can be 40 to 60 dB stronger than the target. A threshold high enough to stop it also stops the target, so the clutter must be removed by its zero Doppler first.

quiz.q: An MTI radar has λ = 0.1 m and PRF = 500 Hz. Find the first blind speed.
An X-band radar (λ = 3 cm) must have no blind speed below 300 m/s. What constant PRF would that need, and what would its unambiguous range be?
quiz.a: PRF ≥ 2v/λ = 2 × 300/0.03 = 20 kHz, giving R<sub>unamb</sub> = c/(2 × 20 000) = 7.5 km: far too short for search, which is why staggered PRF is used.

quiz.q: What is the job of the COHO in a coherent MTI radar?
quiz.a: It is the phase reference at the intermediate frequency: the echo of every pulse is phase-detected against it, so a fixed target gives the same output each pulse and a moving one a changing output.

quiz.q: Why does a double canceller have a wider clutter notch, and why is it not always used?
quiz.a: Its response is 4 sin²(πf<sub>d</sub>T<sub>r</sub>), which rises as f<sub>d</sub>² near zero instead of f<sub>d</sub>, so the notch is wider and rejects spread clutter better. It also cuts slow targets more, and it needs one more pulse of delay.

quiz.q: How does staggering the PRF remove low blind speeds, and what is the cost?
quiz.a: A target is blind only if its Doppler is a multiple of every PRF used, so the first blind speed moves out to (a + b)/2 times the average-PRF value. The cost is slightly poorer clutter cancellation and more complex processing.

beyond: Airborne radars look down on clutter that moves relative to the aircraft, so the clutter spreads in Doppler with angle. Space-time adaptive processing (STAP) cancels it using many antenna elements and many pulses together; ground moving-target indication (GMTI) is its main use. Weather radars use pulse-pair processing to measure the mean Doppler of rain. Search for STAP, GMTI and "moving target detector" to go further.

figure.caption: Single-canceller response 2|sin(πf<sub>d</sub>T<sub>r</sub>)| for the worked examples at λ = 3 cm. At 1000 Hz the blind speeds are 15, 30, 45 m/s and so on; at 1250 Hz they are 18.75, 37.5 m/s and so on. Staggering the two leaves 75 m/s as the first speed blind in both, and at 15 m/s the 1250 Hz interval still passes 1.18.

spec.aria: Graph of canceller output from 0 to 2 against radial speed from 0 to 80 metres per second. A solid sine-arch curve for 1000 hertz touches zero at 15, 30, 45, 60 and 75; a dashed curve for 1250 hertz touches zero at 18.75, 37.5, 56.25 and 75. A point marks 1.18 on the dashed curve at 15, and another marks the common zero at 75.
